noteBlocks.lede: Before any mechanics question can be answered the forces have to be found and named. A force diagram is that list, drawn: one arrow for every push or pull on the body, each with a label. Get the picture right and the equations almost write themselves.
can: Name every force acting on a body and show it as a labelled arrow
Place weight, normal reaction, tension and friction correctly, on the flat and on a slope
Decide what belongs on a force diagram and what does not

noteBlocks.md: Push a book across a table and four things act on it: the Earth pulls it down, the table pushes it up, your hand pushes it along, and the surface drags it back. A force diagram is a way of saying all four at once, in one picture.

noteBlocks.text: 1. One arrow, one label, one force

noteBlocks.alt: A crate of mass 6 kg on a rough horizontal floor. Four arrows leave the crate: R straight up, 60 N straight down, T up to the right along a rope at 26 degrees to the floor, and F to the left along the floor.

noteBlocks.md:
Each force gets a straight arrow drawn from the body, pointing the way that force acts, and a label of its own. Nothing else belongs there: no speeds, no accelerations, no masses.

A label of $6$ kg would be a mass. The force the Earth causes is the weight, $60$ N, and that is what the arrow is for.

noteBlocks.prompt: On the force diagram above, the arrow pointing straight down from the crate is labelled 60 N. Which force is it?
options: the weight of the crate
the mass of the crate
the normal reaction on the crate
noteBlocks.explain: The Earth pulls the crate down with a force of $6 \times 10 = 60$ N. A mass would be in kilograms and is not a force at all.

noteBlocks.text: 2. Weight is $mg$, and it points straight down

noteBlocks.alt: A box of mass 9 kg resting on a slope inclined at 24 degrees. A solid arrow from the box points straight down and is labelled 90 N. A dashed arrow points down the slope and is labelled as not the weight.

noteBlocks.caption: Tilt the surface and the weight does not tilt with it.

noteBlocks.md:
Weight is the pull of the Earth on the body, $W = mg$, and this paper takes $g = 10$ m/s². So a mass of $9$ kg has a weight of $90$ N.

The Earth pulls the same way whatever the surface is doing, so the weight arrow is vertical on the flat and still vertical on a slope. It is drawn from the centre of the body.

noteBlocks.prompt: A box has a mass of 7 kg. Taking $g = 10$ m/s², what is its weight, in newtons?
noteBlocks.explain: $W = mg = 7 \times 10 = 70$ N. The mass is in kilograms; the weight it causes is in newtons.

noteBlocks.text: 3. The reaction leaves the surface at right angles

noteBlocks.alt: The same box on the 24 degree slope. A solid arrow labelled R leaves the box at right angles to the slope. A dashed vertical arrow is labelled as not the reaction.

noteBlocks.caption: On a slope the reaction $R$ is at right angles to the slope, not to the ground.

noteBlocks.md:
A surface cannot pull. The part of its push that comes straight out of it is the normal reaction: on a floor that is vertically up, and on a slope it is at right angles to the slope.

One contact gives one normal reaction, so a body resting on a single surface never carries two.

noteBlocks.title: Why the push is perpendicular
noteBlocks.md: The surface pushes only because the body is trying to sink into it, and sinking in is a movement straight into the surface. So the push that stops it comes straight back out, at right angles. Anything acting along the surface is friction, which is a separate force with a separate label.

noteBlocks.prompt: A box rests on a slope inclined at 24° to the horizontal. In which direction does the normal reaction on the box act?
options: at right angles to the slope
vertically upwards
up the slope
noteBlocks.answer: at right angles to the slope
noteBlocks.explain: Vertically upwards would be the reaction on a horizontal floor. Up the slope is the direction friction or a rope would take.

noteBlocks.md:
Friction acts along the surface and against the sliding, so a block sliding down a slope has friction pointing up it. Turn the motion round and friction turns with it.

A string can only pull, so its tension acts along the string, away from the body. A rough surface gives friction; a smooth one gives none, so none is drawn.

noteBlocks.title: Force diagrams
noteBlocks.why: The same four forces put on several bodies in turn. Watch how each arrow is drawn from the body and labelled before any arithmetic starts.

noteBlocks.prompt: A block slides down a rough slope. In which direction does the force due to friction on the block act?
options: up the slope
down the slope
vertically upwards
noteBlocks.explain: Friction opposes the sliding. The block slides down, so friction acts up the slope, along the surface.

noteBlocks.md:
When two bodies are joined, each one gets its own complete set of forces. The block on the table has a reaction and friction; the hanging block has neither, because it touches nothing.

A light string over a smooth pulley carries one tension all the way along, so both ends take the same label $T$. Two different strings take two different letters.

noteBlocks.prompt: Two blocks are joined by a light string passing over a smooth pulley. The tension pulling one block is labelled T. What label should the tension pulling the other block carry?
noteBlocks.explain: One string carries one tension, so the same letter is used at both ends. A second string would need a second letter.

noteBlocks.md:
An invented force costs a mark as surely as a missing one. The commonest inventions are a second reaction on one surface, friction on a surface described as smooth, and a force drawn down a slope.

That last one matters: the pull down a slope is part of the weight, not a new force. Splitting the weight into components is working, and working belongs beside the diagram.

noteBlocks.title: What the reports keep saying
noteBlocks.md: Two marks for a diagram are among the cheapest in the paper, and about half the entry misses one of them: a reaction left off, friction pointing the wrong way, or a force that was never there.

noteBlocks.prompt: A box rests on a rough slope. Which one of these should not be drawn as a force on the box?
options: the component of the weight down the slope
the normal reaction
the force due to friction
noteBlocks.answer: the component of the weight down the slope
noteBlocks.explain: That component is part of the weight, which is already on the diagram. Drawing it as well counts the same pull twice.

noteBlocks.md:
Name the four forces that turn up on Unit 2 diagrams and draw each as a labelled arrow.
Place the weight vertically from the centre and the reaction at right angles to the surface.
Turn friction to face the sliding, and give one string one tension label.
Give each body of a connected pair its own complete set of forces.
Leave off masses, components and anything that is not a push or a pull.

The opening part of a mechanics question asks you to show every force on the body, on a diagram already printed for you, and it carries two marks: one for roughly half the forces, one for the rest. The first mark is for arrows pointing the right way with labels; the last is for having them all and nothing extra. Stuck? Work round the body: Earth, surface, string, sliding.

workedExamples.stem:
A crate of mass $6$ kg is pulled along a rough horizontal floor by a rope. The rope makes an angle of $26°$ with the floor.

(i) Name the four forces acting on the crate.
(ii) Write down the weight of the crate.

figure.alt: A crate of mass 6 kg on a rough horizontal floor. Four arrows leave the crate: R straight up, 60 N straight down, T up to the right along a rope at 26 degrees to the floor, and F to the left along the floor.

steps.working: The weight is drawn vertically from the centre: $W = 6 \times 10 = 60$ N.
steps.decision: Start with the Earth, because the weight is on every diagram and never depends on what else is happening.

options: Because every body on the Earth has a weight, whatever it is resting on
Because the crate is moving, so it must have a weight
Because the floor is rough, so the weight is larger
whyMenu.explain: Weight depends only on the mass and on $g$. Motion and roughness change other forces, never the weight.

steps.working: The crate touches the floor, so the floor pushes back: the normal reaction $R$, straight up out of the floor.
steps.decision: Work round the body in order — Earth, then surfaces, then strings, then sliding — so nothing is forgotten.

options.text: the normal reaction $R$, straight up out of the floor
options.feedback: The floor pushes straight out of itself, and on a level floor that is vertically up.

options.text: the normal reaction $R$, along the floor against the pull
options.feedback: A surface pushes straight out of itself. A force along the floor is friction, which is the last force in the list.

options.text: no reaction, because the rope lifts the crate off the floor
options.feedback: The rope lifts only part of the weight. The crate still presses on the floor, so the floor still pushes back.

steps.working: The rope pulls along itself, away from the crate: the tension $T$, at $26°$ to the floor.
steps.decision: A string pulls and never pushes, so the arrow leaves the crate along the rope.

options.text: the tension $T$, along the rope at $26°$ to the floor
options.feedback: A rope pulls along its own line, away from the body it is tied to.

options.text: the tension $T$, horizontally along the floor
options.feedback: A rope pulls along its own line. This rope is tilted at $26°$, so its tension is tilted too.

options.text: the tension $T$, and a second force dragging the crate forwards
options.feedback: One rope gives one force. The forward drag is part of the tension, not a second force.

steps.working: The floor is rough and the crate slides forwards, so friction $F$ acts backwards, along the floor.
steps.decision: Friction needs a rough surface and a direction of sliding. Both are given, so it is drawn against the motion.

options.feedback: The crate slides forwards over a rough floor, so friction acts backwards, against the sliding.

options.text: friction $F$, forwards, the way the crate is moving
options.feedback: Friction works against the sliding, so it points the opposite way to the motion.

options.text: no friction, because the rope pulls harder than friction
options.feedback: A rough floor gives friction whenever the crate slides. The size of the pull decides whether the crate speeds up, not whether friction is there.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (i) weight, normal reaction, tension and friction  (ii) $60$ N

figure.alt: A box of mass 9 kg held at rest on a smooth slope inclined at 24 degrees by a rope along the slope. R leaves the box at right angles to the slope, 90 N points straight down, and T points up the slope along the rope.

steps.working: Vertically downwards from the centre of the box: weight $= 9 \times 10 = 90$ N.
steps.decision: Tilting the surface does not tilt the Earth's pull, so the weight arrow stays vertical.

steps.working: Normal reaction $R$, at right angles to the slope.
steps.decision: The surface pushes straight out of itself, so on a slope that is perpendicular to the slope, not vertical.

options: Because the only push a surface makes is the one that stops the box sinking into it
Because the reaction always balances the weight exactly
Because the box is at rest, so every force must be vertical
whyMenu.explain: Sinking in would be movement straight into the surface, so the push that prevents it comes straight out. On a slope the reaction is smaller than the weight.

options.text: the normal reaction $R$, at right angles to the slope
options.feedback: The slope pushes straight out of itself, so the reaction is perpendicular to the slope.
Vertically up is the reaction on a level floor. On a slope the push tilts with the surface.

options.text: the normal reaction $R$, up the slope
options.feedback: Along the slope is where the rope pulls. The slope itself can only push straight out of its surface.

steps.working: Tension $T$, up the slope, along the rope.
steps.decision: The rope pulls away from the box along its own line, and here that line is the slope.

options.text: the tension $T$, up the slope along the rope
options.feedback: The rope lies along the slope and pulls the box towards where it is tied, up the slope.
A rope pulls along its own line, and this rope lies along the slope.
A rope can only pull the box towards whatever it is tied to. It is holding the box up, so it pulls up the slope.

steps.working: No friction: the slope is smooth.
steps.decision: Smooth means the surface offers nothing along itself, so drawing friction would be inventing a force.

options.text: no friction, because the slope is smooth
options.feedback: A smooth surface gives nothing along itself, so nothing else is drawn.
The slope is smooth, so there is no friction. Drawing it would invent a force, which costs a mark.
The slope is smooth, so there is no friction in either direction. Only the rope acts along the slope.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Weight $90$ N vertically down, reaction $R$ at right angles to the slope, tension $T$ up the slope, and no friction

options.feedback: A smooth surface gives no friction, so nothing is drawn along the slope except the rope's tension.
The box touches the slope, so the slope pushes back at right angles to itself.
Every body on the Earth has a weight, and it acts vertically down whatever the surface does.

steps.working: On the $5$ kg block: the normal reaction $R$ up, and the weight down, $5 \times 10 = 50$ N.
steps.decision: Deal with one body at a time. This one rests on the table, so it has a reaction as well as its weight.

steps.working: On the $5$ kg block: tension $T$ towards the pulley, friction $F$ away from the pulley.
steps.decision: The string pulls the block towards the pulley, and the table is rough, so friction opposes that pull.

options.text: tension $T$ towards the pulley, and friction $F$ away from the pulley
options.feedback: The string pulls the block towards the pulley, and friction on the rough table opposes that pull.

options.text: tension $T$ towards the pulley, and friction $F$ towards the pulley as well
options.feedback: Friction works against the pull of the string, so it points away from the pulley.

options.text: tension $T$ towards the pulley, and no friction
options.feedback: The table is rough, so friction acts on the block, against the pull of the string.

steps.working: On the $8$ kg block: tension $T$ up, and the weight down, $8 \times 10 = 80$ N.
steps.decision: The hanging block touches nothing, so it has no reaction and no friction: two forces only.

options: Because a normal reaction needs a surface in contact, and the hanging block has none
Because the hanging block is lighter, so it needs fewer forces
Because the string already includes the reaction
whyMenu.explain: A reaction is a surface pushing back. Nothing is touching the hanging block, so nothing pushes it.

steps.working: The same letter $T$ is used at both ends of the one string.
steps.decision: The string is light and the pulley smooth, so the tension does not change along it.

options.text: the same letter $T$ at both ends of the string
options.feedback: A light string over a smooth pulley carries one tension, so one letter serves both ends.

options.text: a different letter at each end, such as $T_1$ and $T_2$
options.feedback: Different letters are for different strings. One light string over a smooth pulley has one tension all the way along.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: $5$ kg block: $50$ N, $R$, $T$, $F$.  $8$ kg block: $80$ N and $T$.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: which of these is a vector quantity?

options.feedback: A force has a size and a direction, which is why it is drawn as an arrow.
Mass has a size only. It is measured in kilograms and points nowhere.
Time has a size only.
Distance has a size only; displacement is the vector version.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: taking $g = 10$ m/s², what is the weight of a body of mass $5$ kg?

options.feedback: That is the mass with newtons written after it.
That divides by $g$ rather than multiplying.
That uses $g = 9.8$, which this unit does not.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: a line is drawn at right angles to a surface. What angle does it make with that surface?

options.feedback: Right angles and $90°$ are the same thing.
That is half a right angle.
That is a straight line along the surface and back.
That would lie flat along the surface.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: a quantity is drawn on a diagram as an arrow. What does the arrowhead show?

options.text: the direction in which the quantity acts
options.feedback: The arrowhead carries the direction; the label carries the size and the name.
The size is written beside the arrow as a label.

options.text: the point the quantity acts at
options.feedback: That is where the arrow starts, not where it ends.

options.text: the unit the quantity is measured in
options.feedback: The unit belongs in the label.

items.stem: A block rests on a rough horizontal table and is pulled sideways by a string. A student draws the weight, the tension and the friction. Which force has been left out?
items.skill: The normal reaction is never left out

options.feedback: The block touches the table, so the table pushes back: one contact, one reaction.
One string gives one tension. A second one would have to come from a second string.
Mass is not a force and never appears on a force diagram.
The reports name the reaction as the commonest omission of all. Check every contact.

items.stem: A crate is being pushed to the right across a rough floor. In which direction does the force due to friction on the crate act?

options.text: to the left, along the floor
options.feedback: Friction opposes the sliding, so it points against the motion, along the surface.

options.text: to the right, along the floor
options.feedback: That would help the crate along. Friction always works against the sliding.
That is the normal reaction. Friction acts along the surface, not out of it.
Downwards is the weight's direction. Friction lies along the surface.

items.stem: A block of mass $12$ kg rests on a table. How should the downward arrow on the force diagram be labelled?

options.feedback: $12 \times 10 = 120$ N. A force diagram carries forces, in newtons.
Kilograms measure mass. Multiply by $g$ to get the weight the arrow shows.
That uses $g = 9.8$. The front page of this paper sets $g = 10$ m/s².
That divides by $g$. Weight is mass multiplied by $g$.

items.stem: A box rests on a slope inclined at $30°$ to the horizontal. In which direction does the normal reaction act?

options.text: at right angles to the slope
options.feedback: The surface pushes straight out of itself, so it is perpendicular to the slope.
That would be right on a horizontal floor. On a slope the push tilts with the surface.
Along the slope is where friction and a rope act. The reaction is at right angles to it.

options.text: at right angles to the ground below the slope
options.feedback: It is the slope the box rests on that pushes back, not the ground beneath it.

items.stem: A box rests on a slope inclined at $30°$ to the horizontal. In which direction does its weight act?

options.feedback: The Earth's pull does not tilt with the surface. The weight stays vertical.
Part of the weight acts down the slope, but that part is a component, not the weight itself.

options.text: at right angles into the slope
options.feedback: That is the direction of the other component of the weight, and the opposite of the reaction.
The angle of the slope changes the components of the weight, never its direction.

items.stem: Two blocks are joined by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth pulley, and they are accelerating. What is true of the tension?

options.text: it is the same at both ends of the string
options.feedback: A light string over a smooth pulley carries one tension, so one label $T$ serves both ends.

options.text: it is larger at the end nearer the heavier block
options.feedback: The tension does not change along a light string, whatever hangs from it.

options.text: the two ends need different letters
options.feedback: Different letters are for different strings. One string takes one letter.

options.text: it equals the weight of the hanging block
options.feedback: That is only true when the blocks are at rest. If they accelerate, the tension is smaller than that weight.

items.stem: A box slides down a rough slope. Which of these should not be drawn on its force diagram?

options.text: the component of the weight down the slope
options.feedback: The weight is already drawn. Its components are working, and they belong beside the diagram, not on it.
The slope is rough and the box slides, so friction is there, acting up the slope.
The box touches the slope, so the slope pushes back.
The weight is on every force diagram.

items.stem: A candidate draws every force in the right place but puts no arrowheads on the lines. What happens?

options.text: marks are lost, because a line without an arrowhead does not say which way the force acts
options.feedback: A force is a vector; the arrowhead is how the direction is written down.

options.text: nothing is lost, because the positions are right
options.feedback: The reports return to this every year: no arrowhead, no direction, no mark.

options.text: only the weight needs an arrowhead
options.feedback: Every force needs one, and every force needs a label as well.

options.text: the labels can replace the arrowheads
options.feedback: A label names the force and gives its size. The arrowhead gives its direction.

findTheMistake.stem: Cormac labels the forces on a block of mass $8$ kg resting on a rough table and pulled by a horizontal string. His labels:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 labels a force with a mass. Kilograms measure how much matter there is; the arrow shows the pull of the Earth on it, which is $8 \times 10 = 80$ N.
findTheMistake.feedback: Three arrows are named correctly, so the first of the two diagram marks stands. Every label on a force diagram is a force, in newtons. If a mass appears in the question, multiply it by $10$ before it goes on the picture.

findTheMistake.stem: Niamh describes the forces on a crate resting on a slope inclined at $25°$ to the horizontal. Her description:
studentWorking: the normal reaction acts vertically upwards
the rope's tension acts up the slope
the slope is smooth, so no friction acts
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 points the reaction the wrong way. A surface pushes straight out of itself, so on a slope the reaction is at right angles to the slope, not to the ground. Only on a horizontal surface are the two the same.
correction: the normal reaction acts at right angles to the slope
findTheMistake.feedback: Three of the four statements are right, which keeps the first diagram mark. Picture the crate pressing into the surface: the push that stops it comes straight back out, perpendicular to the surface it is resting on.

prompts.prompt: What must every force on a force diagram carry?
prompts.answer: An arrow showing the direction it acts in, and a label naming it or giving its size.

prompts.prompt: How do you work out the weight of a body of mass $m$ kg on this paper?
prompts.answer: Weight = mg, and Unit 2 takes g = 10, so a mass of 6 kg has a weight of 60 N.

prompts.prompt: In which direction does the weight of a body act?
prompts.answer: Vertically downwards, from the centre of the body, whatever the surface underneath is doing.

prompts.prompt: In which direction does the normal reaction on a body act?
prompts.answer: At right angles to the surface the body rests on, pointing away from that surface.

prompts.prompt: In which direction does friction act on a body that is sliding?
prompts.answer: Along the surface, opposite to the direction the body is sliding.

prompts.prompt: A light string passes over a smooth pulley. What can be said about the tension at its two ends?
prompts.answer: It is the same at both ends, so one label serves for both.

prompts.prompt: A box rests on a slope. Which two forces are most often left off the diagram?
prompts.answer: The normal reaction and the force due to friction.

prompts.prompt: Why is the pull down a slope not drawn as a separate force?
prompts.answer: It is part of the weight, which is already drawn: its components are working, not forces.

prompts.prompt: How many normal reactions act on a block resting on one flat surface?
prompts.answer: One: a single contact gives a single normal reaction.

prompts.prompt: What is wrong with labelling an arrow on a force diagram $12$ kg?
prompts.answer: Kilograms measure mass, not force. The label should be the weight, 120 N.

findings.asked: Forces on a block; resolve vertically; F = ma.
findings.wentWrong: A frictional force was invented, labels and arrows were missing; many did not see vertical equilibrium and wrote two-term equations such as R = 17 sin 33; sine and cosine swapped; g omitted; mass used as weight. In the F = ma part most reached '= 5.8a', but some multiplied the acceleration by the weight rather than the mass.
findings.rule: Resolve perpendicular to the motion: every vertical force appears in the equilibrium equation; F = ma uses the mass, never the weight.

findings.asked: Mark the forces on a suspended rod.
findings.wentWrong: Tensions given the same letter; forces or arrows missing; given forces omitted; reactions added; the rod's weight placed midway between the strings instead of at the centre.
findings.rule: A uniform rod's weight acts at its midpoint; each string gets its own tension label.

findings.asked: 'Show that' an acceleration; forces on a block; F = ma with a changed mass.
findings.wentWrong: Working backwards from the given acceleration scored nothing; R was the commonest omission; friction given a fixed value; arrows and labels missing; the mass change (6 kg to 8 kg) missed; sin/cos swapped; equilibrium assumed.
findings.rule: Derive the acceleration from the forces; the normal reaction is always on the diagram.

findings.asked: Forces on a block with a pulling force at an angle; then motion.
findings.wentWrong: Reaction written as 50 with no resolving, or as 30 sin 37; some diagrams had no forces at all; the zero acceleration in part (ii) was not understood.
findings.rule: Mark every force before writing an equation, even if not asked.

findings.asked: Forces on an inclined plane; 'show that' an acceleration; deceleration.
findings.wentWrong: Acceleration substituted rather than derived; weight not drawn vertically; an extra force down the slope; weight components on the diagram were tolerated.
findings.rule: Weight is vertical; its components are your working, not extra forces.

findings.asked: Label the forces on two connected blocks.
findings.wentWrong: Only about half got the diagram: tensions the wrong way, friction missing or reversed, no normal reaction on one block, an extra reaction on the other, and weights labelled with masses (no g).
findings.rule: Weight = mg; friction opposes motion; one normal reaction per surface contact.

findings.asked: Force diagram on a slope; resolve; F = ma.
findings.wentWrong: Friction direction wrong, normal reaction omitted, extra forces, missing arrows - fundamental errors at the end of the paper; sin/cos confusion was less frequent than before.
findings.rule: Two marks for a correct diagram are the cheapest in the paper - draw it properly.

insight.ruleToRemember: Every force is an arrow with a label: weight mg vertically down from the centre, normal reaction perpendicular to the surface, friction along the surface against motion, tension along each string with its own label - and nothing else.
insight.aStarSignal: A clean diagram for a two-body or inclined system that leads straight to correct resolving and F = ma, with 'show that' results derived rather than checked.

checks.detail: Further Mathematics Unit 2, untiered, calculator paper. Identifying and labelling every force on a body: weight mg vertically down, the normal reaction at right angles to each surface in contact, the tension along each string, and friction along a rough surface against the sliding, on horizontal planes, on inclined planes and for two bodies joined over a smooth pulley. No coefficient of friction, no limiting equilibrium, no air resistance and no three-dimensional work.
